slides.text:
Most languages let a function give back one value. A Go function can give back several at once, and the caller receives each of them. You will return pairs, ignore the ones you do not need, and use a second value to say whether the first one is usable.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
first, second = name(input)

name(input):
    give back a, b

slides.text: Instead of one type after the parentheses, the function lists a type for each value it returns, inside their own parentheses. `return` then lists as many values, in the same order.
The caller must receive every value. If it does not need one, it can drop it with `_`, the blank name that Go never asks you to use.

exercises.title: Return two values
exercises.guide: Write a function that gives its two inputs back in reverse order.

chunks.guide: List one type per returned value, in parentheses. `return` gives the values in that order.

notes.text: Two values come back, both strings.

chunks.guide: The caller names one variable for each returned value, in order.

exercises.title: Order two numbers
exercises.guide: Give back the smaller number first and the larger one second.

chunks.guide: The package and the import are already in the file. A function can return from several places, always with the same number of values.
The values arrive in the order the function returned them.

exercises.title: Type and receive
exercises.guide: Give the second returned value its type, and declare the two variables that receive the results.

exercises.title: Ignore a value
exercises.guide: Keep only one of the two values a function returns.

chunks.guide: Quotient and remainder of a division, returned together.
`_` stands where a value you do not need would go. It discards that value, so no variable is left unused.
`_` can sit in any position. Now keep the quotient and drop the remainder.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The first call gives `2, 1`. Swapping those two values again puts them back as `1, 2`.

intro.title: A second value that says more

slides.text: A common use of two values: the first is the result, and the second is a `bool` that says whether the result can be trusted. The caller checks the flag before using the result. The snippet is pseudo code.
You can also **name** the returned values in the signature. They start as zero values inside the function, you assign them like variables, and a bare `return` gives them back.

exercises.title: Result and flag
exercises.guide: Divide two numbers, and say whether the division was possible.

chunks.guide: The second value is a `bool`: `false` when the first value means nothing.

notes.text: A number, plus whether it is valid.

chunks.guide: Assign to variables that already exist with `=`, not `:=`.

exercises.title: Check before using
exercises.guide: Use the flag to decide what to print.

chunks.guide: Half of a number, and whether it was exact.
The flag is a `bool`, so it works directly as a condition.

exercises.title: Type and test the flag
exercises.guide: Give the flag its type, and print the result only when the flag allows it.

exercises.title: Name the results
exercises.guide: Split a number into its tens and its ones.

chunks.guide: Give each result a name. They exist from the start, so you assign them. A bare `return` gives them back.

notes.text: No values listed: it returns the named ones.

chunks.guide: The caller does not see the names. It receives two plain values.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: A `return` that lists values gives exactly those, in that order, whatever the named results hold. The caller gets `2, 1`.
